utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic confirms the statement of facts that was filed with his plea agreement on the 6th of May, 2003, with the qualifications that he provided in his additional statement of facts that he filed with the Popovic Trial Chamber on 17 April 2009. During July 1995, Mr. Nikolic was the chief of intelligence and security of the Bratunac Brigade of the army of the Republika Srpska, or the VRS. Much of Mr. Nikolic's evidence concerns events in Srebrenica and the Bratunac municipalities on the 11th, 12th, and 13th July 1995. Mr. Nikolic also discusses certain activities that occur later in time, such as efforts in September and October 1995 to rebury Bosnian Muslim males who were executed after their capture in or near Srebrenica in July of that year. On the evening of the 11th of July, 1995, Mr. Nikolic was present at two meetings at the Hotel Fontana in Bratunac. Present at the first meeting was General Ratko Mladic, General Radislav Jankovic, and members of the Dutch battalion. The second meeting was attended by General Ratko Mladic, General Radislav Krstic, and other members of the VRS, Colonel Karremans of the Dutch battalion, and a Bosnian Muslim representative named Nedzib Mandzic. On the morning of 12 July, Mr. Nikolic was present outside the Hotel Fontana shortly before a third meeting began. For several minutes, Mr. Nikolic spoke with VRS Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic. Mr. Popovic informed Mr. Nikolic that the Bosnian Muslim women, children, and men not fit for military service would be transported to Muslim-controlled territory. With respect to the fate of the able-bodied Bosnian Muslim men, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic told Mr. Nikolic: "All the balija have to be killed." After the meeting finished that morning, Mr. Nikolic received very similar information from VRS Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric. Subsequently, Mr. Nikolic and members of the Bratunac Brigade military police assisted in the operation to transport Bosnian Muslim civilians away from Potocari and to separate the able-bodied Muslim men from the rest of the persons gathered there. On the 13th of July, 1995, Mr. Nikolic had a conversation with General Ratko Mladic and asked Mladic what would be done with a group of captured Muslims. General Mladic simply drew his hand across his chest in a gesture that indicated to Mr. Nikolic that the captured Muslims would be killed, which is what happened to those captured persons. On the evening of 13 July 1995, VRS Colonel Ljubomir Beara ordered Mr. Nikolic to convey an order to Mr. Drago Nikolic, the assistant commander for security of the VRS Zvornik Brigade. The order was that the captured Bosnian Muslim men, then detained in Bratunac, would be transported to Zvornik, and Drago Nikolic's task was to prepare the facilities and men in Zvornik who would receive these prisoners. Colonel Beara also told Mr. Nikolic that the Muslim prisoners should be detained in Zvornik and executed. Mr. Nikolic's evidence describes how, on the evening of 13 July, he accompanied Colonel Beara to the offices of the SDS party in Bratunac. Mr. Nikolic waited in an outer office while Colonel Beara spoke with Miroslav Deronjic, then the president of the SDS party in Bratunac, and Miroslav Vasic, the chief of the police in Bratunac, in another office. During that conversation, Mr. Nikolic overheard Mr. Deronjic and Colonel Beara argue about the captured Muslim prisoners then detained in Bratunac. Mr. Deronjic wanted all of the prisoners to be transported away from Bratunac, and he opposed the idea that any of the men be executed in Bratunac. Colonel Beara stated that he had very different instructions. And finally, Mr. Nikolic's evidence describes how the goal of VRS forces was to have the Srebrenica enclave empty of Muslims. Your Honour, may I have the Chamber's permission to clarify or highlight several points in the prior testimony of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we continue for just another few seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We've stopped here -- oh, well -- we've stopped here at 01.42.52.1. Mr. Nikolic, there is one person in the foreground with his back to the camera but there are two persons facing the camera. There is a man on the left, a rather tall, thin man, and there is a man more towards the right facing with us a bald head and a moustache. Can you identify those men, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The man on the left is Mr. Karremans, the DutchBat commander, who were in Potocari at the time, and the man with the moustache, the bald person, is Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, who was the chief of the intelligence department with the Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we run the tape just a bit more, please. Stop there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now the man who previously had his back to us has turned to face the camera, and this is at 01.42.55.6. Can you identify the man who is now looking at the camera on the left side of the screen, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's Mr. Vujadin Popovic, chief of the security Department of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We can leave that video-clip now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Continuing with Mr. Kosoric, who you speak about -- who you spoke about in your prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is 65 ter 9507, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say 9570?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, I thought I said 9507.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Nothing is coming up on my screen. I don't know about other persons in the courtroom. Here we are. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this is a document dated the 23rd of May, 1995, from the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff. Do you recall that I showed you this document a couple of days ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What is this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Republika Srpska Army Main Staff, and it concerns the secondment or the request for secondment of officers pursuant to Article 58 of the Yugoslav army law, specifically two officers to be sent to the Army of Republika Srpska. Of course, you can read what it concerns in detail. You can see yourself. I don't need to read it. This is a request for two officers to be sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. The first officer mentioned is Svetozar Kosoric. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At some point in 1995, did you become aware that Svetozar Kosoric became a member of the VRS Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall approximately when that was and the position of Mr. Kosoric?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember how the Drina Corps was being manned and how the recruitment was done for the Drina Corps at that time, which was sometime before the Operation Srebrenica, and from this document one can see when this exactly occurred and when this request was forwarded. So it might have been sometime in June when Mr. Kosoric joined the Drina Corps command and he assumed the duties of chief of the intelligence department of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did you meet Mr. Kosoric at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I really cannot tell you at this moment when was it that when I met him for the first time, but I know it was that the gentleman from the intelligence and security department were active at the time, that they used to come and visit the brigade, but I honestly cannot tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P2518.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been notified that I made two errors when I read out the summary of the witness's evidence, and I would like to correct them please. Both of them involve names. At line 21 [sic] of today's LiveNote, I made a reference to General Radislav Jankovic. That should actually read General Radislav Krstic. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say at line 21 of today's LiveNote, what page are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm referring to page 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And then on page 16, Your Honour, line 6, I referred to Miroslav Vasic and I should have used the name Dragomir Vasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, at page 32915 of your testimony, starting at line 5 through page 32916, line 2, you testify about a Colonel Radislav Jankovic, a Main Staff intelligence officer from the VRS, who, during the time of the events in Srebrenica in July 1995, shared an office with you. Do you recall that portion of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness 65 ter 0949.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, this is a document dated the 25th of April, 1995. Do you recall seeing this several days ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just briefly, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it's similar to the previous one. It is another request sent by the VRS Main Staff to the General Staff of the Yugoslav army to the effect that they asked for the below-named officers from the intelligence department to be sent, and under number 2, we see the name of the officer who shared an office with me during the period that we are discussing, and that is Lieutenant-Colonel Radislav Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall how you first -- or when you first met Radislav Jankovic, and the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I met him the first time, that is Mr. Radislav Jankovic, on the 8th of July, 1995, when General Mladic arrived and he was accompanied by a group of officers from the Main Staff, among them was Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit P2519.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, finally, the last topic, Mr. Nikolic, starting at page 32963 of the -- of your testimony in the Popovic trial, at line 18 and continuing to page 32964, line 10, you describe the resources that were used in the reburial operation during September and October 1995. And on page 32964, at line 6, you make a brief reference to "the number of labourers who were engaged to work." Mr. Nikolic, where did these labourers come from?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, and I think I do, I believe that I was talking about all those who were involved in the reburial operation and the burial of the remains of the Muslims who had been buried in a grave in Glogova. These labourers came and I was referring to them. They came from various quarters. So within the whole operation, involved were members of the Bratunac Brigade, members of the Drina Corps, members of the Bratunac public security stations, members of the Srebrenica public security station, then Bratunac and Srebrenica municipal civilian authorities, and work organisations or companies that had among their resources machinery and those were work organisations from the territory of Srebrenica and Bratunac, and another participant was an engineer battalion of the Drina Corps and the Bratunac utility company. So I was referring to all these men who came from all these sources and who were involved in this operation that was dubbed in my brigade as asanacija, or clear-up operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you mentioned the utilities company from Bratunac. What did the members of the Bratunac utility company do? What was their participation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The workers from the utility company, and I believe that it's clear to everyone what a utility company does in a town, they had machinery and trucks and their workers were mainly involved in the work in the grave itself. That is to say, digging up the grave in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you know where this reburial operation in Srebrenica and Bratunac was planned?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do I know where it was planned?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's my question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. All I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With a great degree of certainty I can say that this operation had not been planned at a local level. According to what I know and based on all the information that I have received to date, indicate that this operation had been planned at the level of the Main Staff and that is how it was presented to the brigade, to my brigade, that is to say, and I testified to this effect in the previous trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, when you refer to the Main Staff, is that the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was referring to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Have you counted the times you answered questions for the benefit of various Defence counsels so far?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking because you probably know that we both must speak slowly and we must make a pause between each of the questions and answers and vice versa in order to ensure an accurate transcript. I've noticed that you have a tendency to speak fast. So do I. Let's do our best to try and help the interpreters and keep the transcript accurate.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to keep track of this, and I hope that everything goes fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would first like to go through the chronology, if I may call it that, of your status. A number of questions about that, although a number of things can be gleaned from the documents that have now been exhibited, above all I'm referring to the joint agreement on facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judging by the speed at which the interpreter is going, two seconds after your warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your indictment was published in March 2002, right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the answer to the question, Mr. Nikolic. Will you please answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were arrested on the 1st of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were charged with genocide, involvement in genocide, extermination, persecution all within the joint criminal enterprise. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: About a year after your arrest you drew up an agreement with the OTP to plead guilty. Pursuant to that agreement, you plead guilty before the Tribunal, guilty of persecution. That was on 7th of May, 2003. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to that agreement, the sentencing ruling was deferred until the close of your number in the Blagojevic case; is that right? And Jokic too.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your conviction came on the 2nd of December 2003, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I will take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another thing that I have come across is that nearly two and a half years later on the 8th of March, 2006, the final judgement came, the 20-year prison term which you are now serving. That was the final sentence, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we look at your -- B/C/S page 4, the English page is 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear the interpreter telling us pages, but he's not telling us pages of what.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is exhibit -- and I think my note is right, P2514. This is it a joint plea agreement annex; the B/C/S page is 4, and the English page is 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to know about paragraph 9. Yes, that's right. This is the plea agreement that you entered into with the Prosecutor of this Tribunal. It reads that, in actual fact, you were willing to cooperate with the Prosecutor and to furnish truthful and complete information whenever so required. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Above all, this is in reference to your knowledge about the events surrounding Srebrenica. The next sentence reads that you agreed to be truthful and candid and to freely answer all questions put to you by members of the Office of the Prosecutor. Also, you agreed to testify at their request in any trial before this Tribunal. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have so far not refused any contact or conversation with The Hague Prosecutor or indeed to appear as a witness before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I've never refused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please, paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It reads here that both you and the Prosecutor agree for all information and testimony provided by you to be absolutely truthful, meaning you must neither minimise your own actions nor fabricate anyone else's involvement. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. You're stating that and what would be the question in it for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question, you personally signed this agreement, right. Can you just respond for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's right I signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you signed the agreement and afterwards as well, when you provided statements to the OTP and when you appeared as a witness before the Trial Chamber, you were fully aware of your obligations under paragraph 11 of this agreement were you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were also aware of the fact that you were in no way to minimise your own involvement or indeed fabricate anything at all about other people's involvement.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that was what you did. You consistently acted in that way after you signed this agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I consistently acted like that, to the extent that I could intellectually or indeed in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I fully understand your response, sir. During your negotiations with the OTP, surrounding your plea agreement, at one point in time you felt that the Prosecutor - at least based on how you felt - was not happy with the information provided by you during those interviews. It therefore crossed your mind that you might be expected to offer something more as opposed to what you had been saying up until that point in time. You testified about that a number of times as far as I remember?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you please ask your question. Try to ask questions. I do have to say this, respectfully. I'm trying to be fair. I wish to answer any and all your questions, but can you please start asking questions and then I start answering. You keep making statements and declarations asking me to confirm. I'm not sure I'm willing to go along with that. Just ask the questions and I'll try to answer all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do believe that that was a question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: One speaker at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One question -- at one point during your negotiations with the OTP, you personally felt or thought that any information that you have been providing up to that point was not sufficient in order to reach an agreement with the OTP. You therefore offered to give them something more, more than you had been giving up until that point in time. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. My answer to your question is at one point in time, and I've testified to this fact countless times so far, at one point in time, there was a moment when negotiations became gridlocked in relation to one particular incident, which I can explain if you would like me to. After the Prosecutor was adamant that I should be there, at one point I became unsettled. That was towards the end of our talks. I'd given them everything that I knew. I told the Prosecutor about everything. And at one point a question came from the Prosecutor, were you involved in that crime? And I said yes. I ordered this and that. After that, and I'm talking about Kravica, the Kravica case, I realised immediately what I had done. I had told an untruth. I asked that the talks cease immediately. We spoke -- I spoke to my lawyers, I told them immediately, "Gentlemen, I actually told an untruth. I want to apologise to the OTP and I want to press on with the talks." That's what happened. And just to be perfectly clear about this, both the Prosecutor and my lawyers, with my consent, needless to say, drew up a statement detailing everything that it said about me telling an untruth about my own involvement in that incident. I apologised to the OTP and we continued with our talks. As talks continued -- or at least I -- I hope, to the extent that I was able, I talked about my crimes, I talked about my own involvement in these crimes and the involvement of other people. I believe I ended up telling the complete truth at least as based on my knowledge and based on my vision of what might -- my experience of what happened. So that's about my additional statement and about any untruths that I may have told.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's easy for both of us to understand what we're talking about. Probably, I'm not sure that the Chamber is aware of all these facts that we are now discussing specifically. Can we please clarify this one thing at a time. As far as I understand, or, rather, let me try to tackle it this way. At one point in time you told the Prosecutors something that was not a truthful and accurate fact, something do with the Kravica incident; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand your last answer, you said this on the spur of the moment, you were revolted because you thought that your talks with the OTP were not proceeding in the right direction. You were in a -- peculiar emotional state and that's why you said it. It wasn't something that was a result of any calculations on your part. You were simply thinking that the Prosecutor was trying to get something more from you as opposed to what you had said up to that point, that was my first question. And then you provided this exceptionally broad answer, just to be perfectly precise. This inaccurate fact or false fact that you then shared with the OTP, was that a result of any calculations that you may have made during your talks with the OTP or was that simply a result of your peculiar emotional state at the time, your revolt?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will answer that question and I'll be perfectly clear about this. The fact remains what I said a while ago. Nevertheless, I have to admit because of the truth. The talks with the Prosecution were nearing the natural end, and I had said up to that point whatever I'd had to say, and I was perfectly clear about this. I said everything that I knew. Any withdrawal from these talks would have been fatal for me, because I'd already given them everything that I knew, and I had said that in my previous testimony. My assessment was that I would not have any avenues open in terms of withdrawing from the talks or stopping the talks, putting a stop to the talks. My assessment was I had to be there. I had to stick with it. I had to remain in these negotiations, and given the situation that I was, that would have been optimal solution for me, so please try not to interrupt that as some form of calculation or speculation. I thought it was the best decision for me at the time and the fairest decision, too. I hope you understand the situation that I was in. Nevertheless, I assumed this responsibility. I never accused anyone else. I apologise. I did make a mistake. I did tell an untruth. I apologised and we continued the talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see this capital letters on the screen, sir, you see these capital letters? That's about you and me. That's about us slowing down, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a very good time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and come back at a quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Mr. Saxon, I see you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we move briefly into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, A question in relation to your last answer. At page 32, line 12, you say that had the talks stopped this would have been a fatal development for you. Why would that have constituted a fatal development for you, as you say, if the talks between you and the OTP had stopped or ground to a halt? Briefly, if you can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: First of all, I'm no lawyer myself. Obviously, this was the first time in my life I was facing a prosecutor or, indeed, an indictment, the first time I've ever stood accused of anything at all. I had no idea at the time, and I took far too long finding my feet, as it were, in this situation. I'm only talking about my own personal conviction. I believed that I had said everything. I was entirely open and forthright about my involvement. This was towards the end of the talks, and I believed at that time that I had run out of arguments defending myself because I had told the Prosecutor everything already about myself, about my involvement, the mode of my involvement. Again, this was my call, my personal assessment. I believed that I would find myself in an unenviable situation. After all these talks and after all information that I provided to the OTP, I believed that I would find myself in a very difficult situation. That was my assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you had remained in your status as an accused, the amount of information had you already provided would have been detrimental to your Defence; is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding, too. Was I right or wrong I don't know. I'm not a lawyer. As I said, it was the assessment that I made at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the talks with the OTP, you wanted to get at the truth about any facts that you were aware of. You wanted to make all this available to the public. That was the ambition behind your admission of guilt; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the talks, I did my best to tell the OTP the truth, the truth that I remembered from back then, the period in relation to which I stood indicted and in relation to the area where -- in which I was deployed to that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we please just look at this, the portion of your testimony in the Blagojevic case, an answer you provided to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please draw up document, it's part of the transcript that's in e-court from the Blagojevic trial. This is 1D03-2995, page 65. This is 2143 in the official transcript of the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is about to come up on our screens will be in English, Mr. Nikolic. It's about the subject matter that we have been discussing right now, what you termed your assessment, your estimate at the time, the assessment that was behind your decision to tell an untruth about a particular fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript page is 65; in e-court, 2143, if our information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Starting with line five, Mr. Karnavas' question. [In English] "Okay. But getting back to what I said, the false information in this story relates to Nikolic, and Nikolic stood to gain the most from the story that Nikolic himself had created and served to the Prosecution [sic]."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Answer: [In English] I did not, Mr. Karnavas, at that point in time think along those lines as to what I would gain and what I will lose. Just then I had decided, since the Prosecution and I were in advanced stage, and since I had conveyed ... the Prosecution everything that I had done and I had been involved in, I simply felt that the agreement should be signed with the Prosecution and that that agreement should be reached, that I should confess my guilt and plead guilty. And within that framework, I made this error, and that is all I can say now." [Interpretation] Do you stand by these words that I have just read back to you, the words you uttered in the Blagojevic case on the 29th of September, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will take your word for it. I'm not receiving any interpretation in my language, but I take your word for it. I stand by it and it is the gist of what I said. I do apologise, just for the Trial Chamber and generally speaking, there is one thing that I'd like to say. I am unable to quote my previous testimonies every time I appear again. But I would like to say that what I said today and what I said in my previous testimony, in my first testimony, that remains the gist. I wanted to reach this agreement, that is true, and I wanted to share with the OTP the truth that I knew. I wanted to share with them what I saw and what I investigated at the time. That was my intension then, as now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go on, Mr. Lukic. Part of the answer by the witness is that he is not getting any translation in a language he can understand. Are we having any problem with the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, we did interpret.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm wondering perhaps whether it's a question of which channel the witness is tuned into? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we help the witness, please. I think it is crucially important --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's crucially important that the witness [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that what happened was something to do with his interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... we can all sing; we cannot all talk at the same time. You're talking, the interpreter is talking, I was trying to talk. I was trying to deal with this problem, and I was trying to say it is crucially important for the witness to hear his previous testimony for him to be able to answer you candidly. And can you reread that passage from that testimony, and can we have the interpretation for the witness being made so that he hears exactly what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, he wants to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I am receiving interpretation in my headphones. Maybe I wasn't accurate and precise enough. I expected that next to the English version I would see on the screen a translation in my language. That is the problem. If that is not supposed to happen, then there is no problem. I heard the interpretation and I understand the gentleman and I trust the interpretation that I have received. I heard everything through my headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. Now, unfortunately, you not see the interpretation in the language that you understand on the screen. You will only hear it here, okay? So if you hear it, that's fine. Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed. You don't have to reread.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nikolic, whenever I put to you portions of your previous testimonies, if you wish to have the reference page, the only way we can do this is to read from the English transcript and then have your comments, and that is similar to the procedure that you had when you had your sessions with Mr. Saxon. Let us now be precise, you did say that you stand by what I read out to you today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak off the microphone while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Lukic? When the witness is speaking, switch off your mic. You are going to speak; you can have it on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point during your negotiations, you offered to the OTP an untrue fact in order to remedy your status that you thought was, at the time, unfavourable. This is my brief conclusion. Just tell me do you agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I already answered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to insist on this any further. From the point of your arrest and you were afforded the rights of an accused, you continuously received material from the OTP in your capacity of an accused.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is the material that is incriminating or exonerating. At any rate, you have received an abundance of material relating to the events that you are testifying about today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And these documents, materials, statement, video footage, these photographs served, among other things, to refresh your memory of the events that happened seven or eight years ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, you may put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And most probably, this material helped you to draw certain personal conclusions about some of the events that you were not aware of at the time, but thanks to the material provided to you, you were able to draw these conclusions concerning people who were involved in those events. To put it simply: After you've seen certain video footage, you establish a connection with what you remember about that and that enables you to draw conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. I knew a lot, even without those materials and statements and documents. And whenever I testified, it, for the most part, referred to what I personally saw or was participant to. So we can agree that the usage and reading of certain statements, orders, or documents helped me just to reinforce and confirm my knowledge. So you can -- you can say that, and that would be my answer to your question, in this particular context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At one point, you had an opportunity to see a photograph taken on the Sandici site, and you thought for a moment that you were in that photograph. Therefore, I assume that, based on that original fact, you tried to remember whether you actually were in Sandici at the time. Later on, with the assistance of your counsel, you established that it wasn't you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Both you and I know what this photograph relates, but let me make it clear. The photograph that I was shown, it was taken out of a set and the person depicted in the photograph resembled me. Without the checking done by my counsel on the ground, I initially didn't know where this photograph had been taken. As soon as I was told that this was taken in Sandici I expressed my doubts, because they told me also the period. I knew for a fact that at that period I was not in Sandici and that made me doubtful. After, I expressed these doubts. But, yes, at the beginning I did say, yes, this man, this soldier in the photograph resembles me or I resemble him. After an investigation conducted on the ground, my counsel found the man who was in the photograph. He confirmed that himself. And then the assertion that it was me in the photograph was rebuked. As for the declaration of guilt, was provided to the OTP later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what I actually asked you a while ago, as an example. After seeing an OTP document, you made an effort to try and remember whether there was any connection between you and their documents, so you tried to think back whether you were in Sandici or not. What I wanted to say is that certain documents supplied to you by the OTP helped you to draw certain conclusions about certain events. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that. That's not correct. Any document provided to me -- or this particular document did not serve me to establish that I won't -- that I wasn't in Sandici. As soon as I was given information about the area where the photograph was taken, I said, No, I wasn't in Sandici at that time. I did pass through Sandici, but I was in a car and nobody could have taken a photo of me in that pose. And nobody could claim otherwise, because I wasn't in Sandici.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. You were also on the OTP list of witnesses in the Popovic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And during the proofing, you were interviewed by Julian Nicholls from the OTP when you were visited in detention unit or, rather, in prison in 2007; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't appear in these proceedings as the OTP witness, but, rather, you were summoned as a court witness in April of this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see another portion of the transcript from this trial, which is not part of the 92 ter package. That's 1D03-4218 in e-court, page 33101, and page 48 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, Mr. Lukic, what do you wanted to do with 1D03-2995?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not tendering it into evidence because I have put only one portion of the transcript, and the transcript is already in evidence. I'm only relying on your guidance and your guidelines, and I think that's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has been read out to you when you testified. This is page 33101 from that same trial. You can't see this on this page. It's actually page 17398. And that's the day when Mr. McCloskey on behalf of the OTP provided certain information to the Trial Chamber and -- which reads as follows. Line 3: "[In English] Mr. President, as I think you are aware, about two weeks ago we had a proofing session with Momir Nikolic. Julian Nicholls met with him and from that proofing session it has arisen that Momir Nikolic has become adverse to Prosecution [sic] case. Adverse to the Prosecution case. He made statements at the proofing session that we don't believe are credible, and in reviewing his overall situation, we have decided, on a balance, to withdraw him as a witness." [Interpretation] You are familiar with this, because this was read out to you during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that point when this interview was conducted with you in prison, you were prepared to appear as an OTP witness in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't put forward any preconditions concerning the OTP 's intention to bring you as an OTP witness.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I never opposed the OTP's intention, because I understand what my obligations are under the agreement that I signed with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the proofing session, did the representative of the OTP show you some documents that you hadn't seen before? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that interview, were you asked to write new information that you hadn't provided previously? Did they ask you some new questions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, they didn't seek any additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the OTP representative tell you at the time that there is contradiction between your present and previous statements and that they were dissatisfied with what you have provided in terms of facts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Lukic. I'm getting a bit lost here. In terms of the witness's agreement with the OTP, he did not undertake this plea bargain. Did he not undertake to testify in favour of the OTP or to testify in support of the OTP case. He undertook to testify truthfully. This passage here does not say that they are dropping him as a witness because he is now contradicting his prior statement. It says he is now giving adverse testimony to the Prosecution's case. If it's truthful, so be it. That's what he has undertook to do. Now, I don't know whether somewhere else in this transcript there is a proposition that he is contradicting his prior statement, but based on the transcript before us, there is no allegation of inconsistent statements. There is an allegation of adverse testimony. I'm not sure whether the question you are putting on is based on this or is based on some other excerpt from this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With the Court's indulgence, may I have a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do have a minute, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what you asked me about, this is only fact that I read from the transcript that was stated by Mr. McCloskey concerning their position why they were unwilling to call this witness. I wanted to check with this witness whether something new occurred during the proofing session without going at all into whether his statement and previous testimonies were truthful or untruthful. This is important for me because of the credibility of this witness, and I'm going to ask some more questions about that later. I am wondering about how interested he was to make the Prosecution satisfied with his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Lukic. But my problem is once you now suggest that he is -- his current statement at the time was inconsistent with a prior statement he had made, then you are mischaracterising the transcript as it stands. The transcript as it stands does not allege an inconsistent statement, a prior statement. It alleges adverse testimony to the case of the Prosecution. The Prosecution -- the Prosecution here just feels that because he is saying something that hurts them, therefore he must be dropped. They are not saying he is untruthful. They are not saying it contradicts a prior statement. This is my problem. So when you talk of inconsistent prior statement, I find that a mischaracterisation of the testimony that is before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I -- just to be -- if I said that there was a discrepancy between his statement and his previous testimony then I made a mistake. That is not what I was trying to talk about. I did not go into the truthfulness of any allegations made at that interview at all. That was not my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... from page 44, lines 25 up to page 45 line 2. "Did the OTP representative tell you at the time that there this is a contradiction between your present and previous statements and that they were dissatisfied with what you have provided in terms of facts?" That was your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will clarify that right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... or did you make a mistake when you said so?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to rephrase that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During a number of different interviews that you had with the OTP over a long period of time, did you ever face a situation where someone from the OTP presented to you a conclusion about your evidence, in terms of saying, "We believe you" or "We do not believe you" in relation to a fact, any fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That is a difficult question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Briefly? I can't do this briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me first please check whether my question is all right by the Trial Chamber. That's just what I -- the only thing that I wanted to know. If this question is not perfectly proper, then I will try and change it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is, I don't see the basis for that question. If -- if the basis for your question is the testimony here, then again you are slightly embellishing the testimony here. They don't say they disbelieve him. They say he is adverse to their case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, to suggest at some stage the Prosecutor might have said to him, "I don't believe you," is to take it a step further. A legitimate question would be, Did at some stage the Prosecutor say to you, "Your answer is hurting our case"? That's what the Prosecutor said to the Court. Okay, I beg your pardon. I must withdraw my statement. I must withdraw. There is a passage to that effect; I'm awfully sorry. I only remembered what you had put to the witness, but I see on reading further there is something. My apologies. That last question -- [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: If I understand your question correctly, I will try to provide an answer. The Prosecution and I had countless conversations. There was never a single conversation in which we had the exact same opinions, me on the one hand and the OTP on the other, about a whole range of different issues. I had my convictions, my opinions which I freely stated to the OTP. Believe me, whenever I talked to the OTP I never tried to say what I believed they wanted to hear. I always tried to say what I thought was the truth. I always tried to provide my understanding of whatever problem the Prosecution wanted to know about. Along these lines, I think our talks were extremely fair. I never had anyone from the OTP making any complaints about me. They didn't praise me either, but they didn't have any particular objections to raise to what I was saying or the way in which I was putting it. That, in principle, would answer your question. As to what I was actually talking about, what we were talking about during the proofing in Finland played into the OTP's hands or not. The manner in which I explained certain problems, now that is not something that I can say. The OTP never told me what you asked me about or what you suggested: "Mr. Nikolic, this is adverse to the OTP's case," they never said. Nor indeed did they express an opinion to the effect that anything I was saying was favouring their case. They just told me that I had to say whatever I felt I had to say. This, in the briefest possible terms, would be an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you heard in court when it was read back to you, what Mr. McCloskey had previously told the Trial Chamber, I bet you didn't like it when you heard that assessment of the OTP when they said why they chose not to call you; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's right, I didn't like it. I said then - and I think when I eventually appeared towards the end of my testimony I had another opportunity to reiterate that I simply said that I had never refused to appear. I also said there was nothing adverse in terms of my disposition towards the OTP, nothing hostile. I had no problem with that. I was perfectly willing, in keeping with my duties and obligations under the agreement, to appear as a witness whenever summoned by the OTP. That was my answer in court, the last time I appeared, and it still is today. I can only repeat that. I'm willing to appear as a witness whenever summoned by either of the parties, and all I will be talking about all my evidence will be about the truth as I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What you really care is for the truth to be established about what occurred in Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course I do. I am trying to contribute to that. I'm trying to help get at the truth about what happened, about the crime, within my powers and to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You would also like to see established the involvement of each and every individual in those events, right? Briefly. Let's try to speed things along a little.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do care about that too. I admitted my on responsibility, and I would like for the responsibility of everyone else who was involved to be established as well, and obviously I know about those too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yet you refused to appear as a witness before the national court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in relation to these same events; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That is not right. I appeared there twice, as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you refused to go there to testify because you believed that that wasn't part and parcel of your agreement with the OTP; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Again, you appear to have been misinformed. Nobody asked me to go to Sarajevo. They wanted me to testify via videolink from Helsinki, which is exactly what I did. The first time around I refused to appear as a Prosecution witness simply because I had been given no documents at all, nothing apart from the summons to appear as a witness. On the other hand, I believed that I should be given information or an indication as to what I would be testifying about. I believed that this required some proofing, and I also believed that since under my agreement with the OTP I had no obligation to appear before a court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which, by the way, didn't even exist at the time. I believed it was the duty of the BiH prosecutor to at least come over and ask me whether I was willing to participate in those trials. On the other hand, I did not wish to not appear at all and then I asked to be the court's witness. And that is the capacity in which I appeared in the first trial there. As for the second trial, they told me what I would be testifying about. I was provided documents, and in that second trial I eventually appeared as a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My information suggests that you were not willing to testify because that wasn't in the terms of your agreement with the OTP. Your agreement with the OTP was only about appearing before this Tribunal. Do you remember ever saying anything like that? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think that is true. But what I'm telling you now is that, as a matter of fact, I did appear as a witness there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was never in doubt.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Fair enough then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The statement that has been exhibited - and, Your Honours, I'm talking about Exhibit P2513 - is a statement that you hand-wrote in Finland, in prison before appearing in the Popovic case. If I understand correctly, the substance of that statement is about your clarification of certain facts from your admission of guilt. You drew up this statement in order to adjust certain statements or the allegations made in your previous admission, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You know that each time one appears as a witness before a court one testifies under oath, and perjury has certain consequences. You handwrote this statement, despite which you are prepared and willing to bear any consequences as if the handwritten statement had been provided under oath, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you are saying and I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's not intention of the Defence to tender 1D03-4218?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, same as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go through a couple of things. Can we have page 2 in the B/C/S and the English page is right there at the bottom, Prosecution Exhibit P2513. That is your statement. What shall I call it? Yeah, that's probably the best. Handwritten statement to be perfectly accurate; right? What I want to know about is when as a matter of fact you explain paragraph 1 of the admission statement and here you go on to say: "The intentions of the VRS, the first intention was to" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just direct us exactly on the page where you are reading. Okay, I can see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Halfway down the page, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "To physically separate two enclaves, the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica, to liberate the Zeleni Jadar-Jasenovac-Milici road and, in phase 2, to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the town area. The forcible removal of the entire Muslim population from Srebrenica was the result of the fall of the enclaves and subsequent decisions." I assume, since you provided a clarification, that -- and let me try to be accurate. When the operation was launched, Krivaja 95, that's what we'll be calling it; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This was the plan. What you said here, that was the original plan for that operation; right? Meaning to physically separate the two enclaves, and in stage two to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the area of the town itself, the restricted area of the town itself. Is my understanding correct, when Krivaja 95 began that was the principle objective and only after the fall did all the other things --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could counsel please speak up, speak directly into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, just read what the interpreter has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time the attack was launched on the enclave, you will agree with me that there was no talk of a forcible removal of the population or any crimes when the attack on the enclave started, when the objective was to do what you just said, to separate the enclaves and to reduce the Srebrenica enclave to the area of the town itself; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, you're asking me as if I had been involved in the planning of this operation. I can only tell you about my level.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You're asking about my level, my level, my brigade, my organ, we were not discussing the issue that you just raised. Was this perhaps discussed at a level higher up? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then what you go on to state about the intention of the VRS, these are facts that you had at your level, the brigade level, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the brigade level, you were not receiving any information from higher up about any further consequences of the attack on the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When the attack on the enclave began at your level, the Bratunac Brigade, you did not receive any information from higher up receiving something, for example, from the corps, intelligence organ, information that there would be a forcible removal of the population when the attack began. You did not receive any information like that, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You can't have any information like that at a moment when the operation is already under way. To be perfectly clear, please, these issues are subject to assessments; the results and consequences of an attack carried out in a certain area. There are assessments that are made prior to an attack as to what might happen. You can't expect someone to inform you to provide reliable facts as to what would perhaps happen. You make an assessment. Every time you make an assessment you must make certain allowances or predictions knowing what forces will be deployed, knowing what the objective of the operation is, you have to try and envisage the possible consequences. What I wrote here, what eventually happened after the actual combat that was part of the operation. There was another part of the operation which was the forcible removal. Forcible removal was a result of decisions taken following the combat part. That is what I tried to explain, to make that perfectly clear to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at a document, which is 65 ter 2529.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you're going see it shortly and the screen, but I think that Mr. Saxon has already shown this document to you during proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. I think it's placed under seal. [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall first look at page 1 and then look at the last page, and we will just briefly comment on this document. This is from the Drina Corps command, entitled an order for active BD, which I believe stands for combat activities, dated the 2nd July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the last page first to see who signed the document and then we will go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recognise this signature and do you know this individual, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I know who the corps commander was at the time. Therefore, I know who signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was General Zivanovic, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go back to page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's read number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please scroll the document down a bit, please, so that we can see who the recipient is, and this is right beyond the title.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, was this order sent to your Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic says in this first part, I'm reading the paragraph under the paragraph numbered 1. "We believe that in the forthcoming period that in -- the enemy will intensify offensive activities ... in the area of responsibility of the DK." DK is the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Mainly in the Tuzla-Zvornik and Kladanj-Vlasenica axis with simultaneous activity by the 28th PD," I suppose that stands for "infantry division," "... from the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa in order to cut the DKZO," I suppose which stands for area of responsibility of the Drina Corps, in two, and linking the enclaves with the central part of the territory of the former B and H held by the Muslim forces. The next paragraph. "During the last few days, the Muslim forces from the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica were particularly active." They are infiltrating DTG, which stands for sabotage and terrorist groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: "Who are attacking and burning unprotected villages, killing civilians and small isolated units around the enclaves of Zepa and Srebrenica. They are persistently trying to persistently trying to link up the enclaves and open a corridor to Kladanj" and so on and so forth. This is a rather long document. On the next page we can see what the intelligence organs' tasks were. After looking at this document with the OTP, do you remember whether there was any discussion in your command about this order to launch an attack which was as part of a Krivaja 95 operation, particularly the part pertaining to your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is an order to -- for active operations. You can see who it is addressed to, and the Bratunac Brigade indeed received this order too. Actually, I'm confirming that based on what I see on the screen. Before I came to The Hague and before I was given documents by the OTP, I had never seen this order before. Following this order, and that is a standard procedure, combat documents have to be drawn up. So after this order had been received, the Bratunac Brigade did not draw up complete combat documents for the operation in Srebrenica and its participation concerning its role. Therefore, what I know is that an order was prepared by the Bratunac Brigade, I think for active combat operations, that laid down the tasks of the Bratunac Brigade units, mainly infantry battalions. So the Bratunac Brigade commander decided to issue tasks in that way. Concerning this order for active combat operations, as I said, I hadn't had an opportunity to see it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now given that you were an intelligence officer at the time, you are familiar with the facts that I just read and that Mr. Zivanovic makes reference about the situation in the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, these are typical facts and typical language used in these kind of orders, so I'm familiar with these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D134.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you going to move away from this topic? It's just that I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please, ask the question. Feel free to interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, at page 54 in today's transcript, you said, and starting from line 9, "You're asking about my level, my level, my brigade, my organ. We were not discussing the issue that you just raised. Was there perhaps discussed an a level higher up? I don't know." Now, this is after you have said -- after had you been shown your statement that you wrote from Finland, in which you told the intentions of the VRS. My question to you is: At your level, at your organ, at your brigade, where did you get the information that you wrote in your statement, in the statement that you made in Finland? As to the intentions of VRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I already answered this question, but I will endeavour to give you an answer in the best possible way I can. The intentions of the Army of Republika Srpska, or, rather, the intentions underlying the attack on Srebrenica, at the time, I primarily understand, as intentions concerning the -- the enclave of Srebrenica. Immediately before the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, the Bratunac Brigade was visited by the then corps commander, General Zivanovic, who was en route to some other destination. That happened about two weeks before the attack. That was not an official meeting. He actually came to his native village. He just dropped by to the brigade and he spoke on that occasion about what was going to happen in the forthcoming days. And he said that these two enclave, Zepa and Srebrenica, had to be separated physically and that had to be done urgently, that Srebrenica had to be reduced to an urban area, and these were the arguments that I knew about at the time. When the counsel asked me about that, I said that I never understood and realized that objective of the VRS was as I stated in the statement. I was talking about the information that I had available to me two weeks prior to the operation, and this is indeed what happened in the days after the commencement of the operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Is your -- your question -- your answer to my question that you got this information from Commander -- I forget his name. The commander of the ... sorry. Zivanovic. Is that your short answer? Is that what Zivanovic told you two weeks prior to the attack as what the intentions of the VRS were? A yes or no will help.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the information I had and that was the first time I heard about what was going to happen. Yes, I heard it for the first time from General Zivanovic about the intentions concerning Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And those intentions are as you put them in your statement in Finland, your written statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The intention was to separate the two enclaves and also everything else that I put in my statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic, you may proceed. I'm sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now going to discuss your encounter with -- or rather the events that took place outside Hotel Fontana on the 12th. Your encounter with Mr. Popovic and the conversation that you had which you have described and which has now become -- became -- become a part of the transcript of this Tribunal, happened sometime before the 10.00 meeting which was held in Hotel Fontana; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This conversation of yours with Popovic lasted, according to you, five, seven, ten minutes at the most.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look now at page -- just a moment. Page of the transcript, which is not part of the 65 ter package. And that's document 1D03-4058, page 4. I gave the wrong number of the page. It seems I gave the wrong page number. What I actually need is transcript page, official transcript page, 32918. It is possible, after all, that this is part of the document P52512. Yes, we have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is your testimony, Mr. Nikolic, and you say the following, about what Popovic told you. I'm going to read it. I'll start from line 1: "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... he also said that so-called screening would be carried out in order to separate able-bodied men, to identify those who had committed or who are suspected of committing war crimes, et cetera. However, at this point in time I really have to provide an additional information. "After all this, something happened that was absolutely never planned nor did I grasp from my conversation with Mr. Popovic that something could happen. Expect in the first convoy, our -- not only able-bodied men were separate, but all, all men who were in Potocari were separated from their families and put on bus -- actually, first detained in Potocari. "Therefore, I asked Mr. Popovic what was going to happen to these men ..." [Interpretation] I'm not going to read any further. What I'm interested in is the following. When did you find out with respect to this conversation with Popovic that you had, that all men from Potocari would be separated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I found out that morning, then, what, roughly speaking, would be happening, what the next tasks were, and what would become of the men who were still in Srebrenica. At this point for the first time officially, I believe, Mr. Popovic was officially my superior. If you look at the chain of command. This was the first time I found out about what in the roughest of terms would be happening. Even prior to this conversation I assumed what would be happening to those people there, that they would be leaving the enclave, but this was the first I heard of what you have just been asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you had not found out about the separation of all men before you talked to Popovic, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My reading of the transcript of your evidence is this. I see you asking Popovic what would become of those men because you had just found out that all the men were being separated.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, that is a misreading. If that is your understanding of my evidence, I think that is false. I had asked Popovic beforehand. A meeting took place before any operation to do with this transport even began. The operation itself began between 1.00 and 2.00 p.m. and the meeting outside the Fontana Hotel was held at about 10.00 a.m. that same day. The conversation occurred before any transport at all occurred. Any knowledge I had about their status and what else would be happening as part of this operation was from about the -- was from before the 10.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your reason for asking Popovic what would become of those men, if you had received no information at all about that prior to this?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Popovic what would be the next steps taken about the men, because there were between 25.000, 40.000 persons in Potocari. That was my evidence. If it reads otherwise then it must be about translation. I asked Mr. Popovic what steps would be taken next, about the people who were in Potocari, between 25.000 and 30.000 of them, including men.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak into the microphone, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... of which the portion of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... speak into the microphone, and I'm asking you to also try and find a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You looked through a portion of the transcript with Mr. Saxon. You entered certain corrections. I'm reading what you see in the transcript. I don't think any corrections were made in relation to that portion. If I'm wrong, I'm sure Mr. Saxon can put me right -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... what was going to happen to these men because, to be honest, not even then I couldn't understand why these men were being set aside. [Interpretation] This is a sentence that you actually uttered and never corrected. It's in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only say one thing. I know exactly what I said. I know exactly what happened. If an error was made in the transcript, I didn't read the transcript myself. There was an interpreter who read it for my benefit. The interpretation that I received was accurate. And it amounts to this. After the meeting with Popovic and during our conversation I asked what the next steps would be that would be taken in Potocari. He then told me that all the women and civilian -- that's what I said, and I can only repeat it now. And that was my evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move that we now take a break.
